newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco talks resume as jury deliberates.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco talks resume as jury deliberates.

text.p: A Florida jury's deliberations in a widely-watched tobacco case are boosting the pressure on cigarette makers as they resume negotiations Monday with state attorneys general aimed at resolving mounting litigation.

The threat of a possible negative verdict following the recent court ruling upholding the Food and Drug Administration's authority to regulate tobacco as a drug has raised the stakes in the talks and the industry has agreed to make a number of concessions.

If a settlement can be reached the tobacco industry would stop billboard advertising, end vending machine sales and finance anti-smoking programmes, according to published reports. On Monday, USA Today reported that the cigarette makers would also accept workplace bans on smoking and stricter cigarette package warning labels.

In making such concessions, the industry hopes to settle some of the suits against it or at least put a ceiling on its liability. With state attorneys general unified in stance that a settlement will exclude blanket immunity for the tobacco industry, total protection from lawsuits is not an option for cigarette makers.

The attorneys general are suing the industry to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers. The first of the trials is scheduled for July in Mississippi. The industry also faces hundreds of individual suits filed by smokers and their families including the current Florida trial as well as a number of class actions.

The industry, which began negotiating directly with the attorneys general early last month, has been hit with some significantly harsh blows recently. The most damaging was last month's ruling by a Greensboro, N.C., federal judge, who once represented tobacco growers as a private attorney, that held the FDA has the power to regulate tobacco.

Although the judge said the FDA did not have the authority to regulate advertising of cigarettes, the Supreme Court refused a few days later to hear a challenge to Baltimore's law restricting placement of tobacco billboards.

Legal experts predicted the move would help strengthen efforts by local municipalities to restrict tobacco advertising and just last week a proposal was made to the New York City Council to ban tobacco billboards and promotions near schools and other locations where children gather. Washington State's King County, which encompasses Seattle, is expected to vote on a similar proposal on May 30.

While these losses are pressuring the industry to find a solution soon, some anti-tobacco forces believe the defeats make a settlement premature or even unnecessary. Some health groups in particular have opposed an accord.
Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey even wrote his colleagues last Friday urging them against acting too hastily.

"Is this the right time to settle?" he wrote. "Frankly, it may not be," Humphrey wrote. "We have strong cases and if we try and win even a few, we will have brought the industry not just to the table, but to its knees."

Even as the industry and attorneys general resume their talks, the Jacksonville, Fla., jury will be deliberating whether R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings, can be held liable for a smoker's death.

The case is being widely-watched because one of the plaintiff's lawyers is Norwood "Woody" Wilner who won a verdict against Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., a unit of B.A.T Industries PLC, last summer causing tobacco stocks to plummet. If he should win the current case, many legal experts believe it will signal that public opinion has turned against the industry that had for years won almost every case.
Even if the industry is not held liable in this trial, Wilner has filed about 300 other cases and the odds are that he would probably win some of the other suits.
